rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on defensible ground and makes the ugly proof gaps part of the strategy, not decoration. Its line, "Who actually supplies the compounded semaglutide?" is exactly the question a real pharma or safety reporter will ask first. B has useful bones, but "Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs, patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead" invents patient behavior the fact block does not give it; that is how a decent angle set gets itself fact-checked in public.
gaps_in_A: "A newly profitable Hims & Hers bets its margins on compounded weight-loss drugs" overreaches slightly. The update says publicly traded and recently profitable; it does not give margin exposure or revenue contribution.
"a model other telehealth players may follow" is plausible but speculative. A correctly asks for proof, but the headline-level category frame is still ahead of the facts.
"Decay: 4hr" on the FDA angle is too cute. Regulatory risk is not a kitchen timer, and the update gives no specific FDA action date that justifies that precision.
"copy of a blockbuster drug" is a little loose. The update supports compounded semaglutide at lower prices, not a clean branded-drug-copy claim with a named comparator.
gaps_in_B: "Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs, patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead" is the big miss. No patient, adoption, affordability barrier, or switching behavior appears in the update.
"A newly profitable Hims & Hers doubles down" uses a blacklisted cliche and implies a prior GLP-1 bet the supplied facts do not establish.
"Freshly profitable Hims & Hers bets its next act" pads the set with a second markets/regulatory-risk wrapper. It is not distinct enough from the earlier FDA-risk angle to earn its own slot.
"gray-market-adjacent story" is loaded and legally sloppy. The facts say compounded, FDA-flagged risk, and unnamed supply source; they do not say gray market.
